newsitem.title: INDIA: India must correct fiscal imbalance - World Bank.
newsitem.headline: India must correct fiscal imbalance - World Bank.

text.p: World Bank President James Wolfensohn said on Sunday that India must aim to bring down its budgetary deficit, and broaden domestic financial markets, to fund infrastructure projects.

"The way in which India will take off is when you can mobilise your own resources for infrastructure. Now in order to do that, you've got to pull down your fiscal imbalance," Wolfensohn told a news conference in the Indian capital.

India aims to cut down its budgetary deficit to 5.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the current fiscal year ending on March 31. The budgetary deficit stood at 5.9 percent in 1995/96 (April-March).
He said India, with a high savings rate of 22 to 24 percent, must broaden its financial system to mobilise funds for infrastructure projects.
India is facing a slowdown in its infrastructure sectors in the current year and industry leaders have warned that an infrastructure bottleneck could choke economic growth.
India aims to achieve a GDP growth of 6.6 percent in 1996/97 against 7.0 percent last year.
Wolfensohn arrived in India, the largest recipient of World Bank money, on October 12 in Bombay on a week long visit to the country.
He said that the Bank and the Indian government held discussions on infrastructure, particularly the power sector.

Wolfensohn said that International Finance Corporation (IFC), the Bank's private sector lending wing, was trying to generate interest among foreign investors for investing in sectors where the Indian government wanted.
The World Bank and the Indian government have agreed to review all Bank projects under implementation in the next four to six months.
"We have agreed in the coming four to six months we will take a look at every single project ...." Wolfensohn said.
He said that the progress and implementation of Bank projects in India must be monitored and brought under rigorous management control.
The slow implementation of many Bank projects and tardy utilisation of Bank funds by the Indian government have lately come under criticism.
India gets about $15 billion a year in World Bank loans.
"Let us not pre-judge," Wolfensohn said, adding that after a review of the projects, the World Bank and Indian government would be able to find ways of making things work better.
Wolfensohn said that he did not discuss the subject of corruption with the Indian government.
But he warned: "On World Bank projects, if there is any evidence of corruption, we will just close them."
"The single most impeding factor in terms of development is corruption. It distorts the economic basis on which you can build things," Wolfensohn said.
He said if any nation was willing to discuss issues like procedures, transparency and governance with the World Bank, it was prepared to stand by it.
